title: Mycenaean sword and Carpathian axes found together in a Macedonian lake village
dek: A pile-dwelling settlement on Lake Dojran yields weapons from the Aegean and the Carpathians, plus a metallurgist's workshop, all from the middle of the second millennium BC.
body: At Mrdaja, a settlement built on wooden platforms above Lake Dojran in North Macedonia, archaeologists have uncovered a bronze rapier of Mycenaean type lying near a socketed battle axe with Carpathian parallels and a double-sided Kilindir axe known from central Macedonia. The weapons surfaced during the 2026 excavation season around a structure that also held moulds for casting double-edged bronze axes, hammers, and other metalworking tools.

Three dwellings dated to the middle of the second millennium BC were exposed this season. One building stands out: its floor area produced extensive evidence for bronze production, leading the team to suggest it belonged to a metallurgist or served as a specialised workshop. The concentration of weapons around this same structure has prompted the researchers to consider whether they mark an episode of conflict at the settlement, though the depositional circumstances remain uncertain.

The Mycenaean-style sword points toward connections with the Aegean world. The ribbed socketed axe finds its closest parallels in the Carpathian region hundreds of kilometres to the north. The Kilindir axe links the site to traditions in central Macedonia. Together the assemblage suggests that the community at Mrdaja participated in networks moving objects, technologies, and ideas across the prehistoric Balkans.

Beyond the weapons, the workshop area yielded moulds for double-edged axes and traces of cinnabar on architectural elements, hinting that parts of the building's facade were coloured red. Raised circular features surrounded by concentric rings and a spiral frieze decorated the exterior, an elaboration that has led the archaeologists to ask whether metalworking held particular symbolic or social weight within the village.

Ceramic vessels engraved with solar symbols appear repeatedly in the Mrdaja assemblage, possibly marking religious or symbolic practice. An amulet made from a sea snail shell, coiled bronze wire rings, and ceramic spindle whorls round out the finds. Some ceramic objects may have served as fishing weights, a reminder that the lake itself remained a daily resource.

The settlement's layout, houses on platforms linked by footbridges, reflects a life adapted to the lakeshore. Yet the combination of local fishing gear, specialised metal production, and far-flung weapon types argues against a simple subsistence economy. Mrdaja appears to have been a node in a wider system of exchange and craft specialization around 3,500 years ago.

No verified academic paper accompanies the HeritageDaily report. The dating rests on typological parallels for the weapons and pottery, and on the stratigraphic position of the dwellings within the mound. Radiocarbon or dendrochronological results from the 2026 season have not been published.
doesnt_show: The finds do not show whether the weapons were used in combat, traded as prestige goods, or deposited ritually. They also do not yet show absolute calendar dates for the destruction or abandonment of the excavated dwellings.
settle: Published radiocarbon or dendrochronological dates from the workshop floor and weapon layer, plus use-wear analysis on the blades, would clarify the chronology and the circumstances of deposition.
